title: The Garment That No One Can Borrow
paragraphs:
The Garment That No One Can Borrow
The Lesson I Learned from Revelation 16:15 That Changed the Way I See Salvation Forever
There are verses in Scripture that comfort us.
There are verses that inspire us.
And then there are verses that suddenly stop us in our tracks—verses that feel as though heaven itself interrupts our routine and asks a question our soul has been avoiding.
Revelation 16:15 is one of those verses.
Right in the middle of God's judgment upon the rebellious world—between bowls of wrath, cosmic upheaval, and the gathering of kings for Armageddon—Jesus suddenly speaks.
Almost as if He refuses to let His own people become distracted by prophecy while forgetting the condition of their own hearts.

"Behold, I am coming like a thief! Blessed is the one who stays awake, keeping his garments on, so that he will not walk about naked and people see his shame."
(Revelation 16:15, NASB 1995)
Ἰδοὺ ἔρχομαι ὡς κλέπτης· μακάριος ὁ γρηγορῶν καὶ τηρῶν τὰ ἱμάτια αὐτοῦ, ἵνα μὴ γυμνὸς περιπατῇ καὶ βλέπωσιν τὴν ἀσχημοσύνην αὐτοῦ.
"Idou erchomai hōs kleptēs; makarios ho grēgorōn kai tērōn ta himatia autou..."
τηρῶν (tērōn) means guarding, preserving, carefully keeping.
Jesus is not speaking about fashionable clothing.
He is speaking about spiritual readiness.
The image immediately brought me somewhere else in Scripture.
In Matthew 22, Jesus tells a parable about a king preparing a wedding banquet for his son.
Others mistreat and even murder the king's servants.
Both good and bad are welcomed.
Until the king notices one man.

"Friend, how did you get in here without wedding clothes?"
(Matthew 22:12)
Because he cannot explain why he thought he didn't need it.

"For many are called, but few are chosen."
(Matthew 22:14)
For years I wondered why the garment mattered so much.
The Bible often explains the Bible.

"He has clothed me with garments of salvation; He has wrapped me with a robe of righteousness."
(Isaiah 61:10)
Religion always tries to dress itself.
In Revelation, Jesus again speaks of garments.

"They will walk with Me in white, because they are worthy."
(Revelation 3:4)
Later John sees heaven filled with believers wearing white robes.

"These are the ones who came out of the great tribulation. They washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb."
(Revelation 7:14)
The greatest scandal becomes the greatest cleansing.
Only the Gospel could write such a sentence.
Even Revelation 19 prepares us for another wedding.
The marriage supper of the Lamb.
John immediately explains what it represents:
"For the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints."
This does not contradict salvation by grace.
Scripture consistently teaches that genuine faith produces transformed living.

"For by grace you have been saved through faith... not as a result of works."
(Ephesians 2:8–9)
Yet the very next verse continues,

"For we are His workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works."
(Ephesians 2:10)
Good works never purchase the garment.
They reveal that Christ has already clothed us.
This is why Revelation 16:15 struck me so deeply.
Jesus isn't telling believers to manufacture their own righteousness.
He is calling them to remain awake, faithful, and persevering in Him.

The command to "keep your garments" echoes the biblical call to remain steadfast in Christ, whose righteousness alone covers His people. Those who truly belong to Him continue in faith, repentance, and obedience—not to earn salvation, but because they have been transformed by grace.
The greatest danger isn't open rebellion.
The man at the wedding had proximity to the King.
Far fewer have truly been clothed by Jesus.
The wedding garment cannot be borrowed from parents.
It cannot be inherited from a Christian nation.
It cannot be purchased by generosity.
It cannot be earned by morality.
It cannot be stitched together with good intentions.
It is received only through repentance and faith in the crucified and risen Christ.
That is why Revelation inserts this warning in the middle of judgment.
Prophecy is not given to satisfy curiosity.
It is given to awaken holiness.
Jesus interrupts the chaos to remind His Church that His return will expose every counterfeit confidence.
The question is not whether we have impressed people.
The question is whether we have been clothed by Christ.
"Clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ."
The believer is wrapped in the righteousness of Another.
The cross is where our filthy garments were exchanged for His perfect righteousness.
The resurrection is God's declaration that the garment fits forever because Christ Himself secured it.
This is why our ministry exists under one simple conviction:
Every page of Scripture tells that story.
Joshua the high priest stood before God wearing filthy garments.
The prodigal son returned covered in failure.
The cross looked like history's greatest scandal.
Yet through it, God clothed sinners with eternal righteousness.
If this message has stirred your heart, don't let it end with quiet agreement.

Your support is not merely helping a page grow; it is helping the Gospel reach more hearts with faithful, Christ-centred teaching that points people to repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and the finished work of Jesus. If your desire is to glorify God with the resources He has entrusted to you, supporting Gospel-centred ministry is one practical way to participate in making Christ known.

Because when the King arrives, no one will ask what titles we carried, how many followers we had, or how impressive our achievements appeared. Heaven's question will be infinitely simpler—and infinitely more important:
The garment of grace cannot be woven by human hands—it is received with empty hands at the foot of the cross.
